extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101, including how to identify judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, mental processes, laws of nature, products of nature) and apply the Step 2A/2B (Prong One/Two) framework and related procedures (Pathways A–C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim recites a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are essentially mental processes (e.g., analysis or manipulation of data that can be performed mentally or with pen and paper) are abstract ideas and can be ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should look to the specification to determine whether claimed steps are described as being performable mentally (examples: CyberSource (listing transactions), Flook (computations by pencil and paper), University of Florida Research Foundation v. General Electric (pen and paper methodologies), Symantec (screening messages that can be performed by a human)). If the claim limitations can be performed mentally, they qualify as a mental process-type abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: A claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims can recite a mental process even if claimed as being performed on a computer; the fact that a computer is recited does not automatically avoid the mental process exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim in light of the specification. Review whether the specification describes the invention as a concept performed in the human mind and the applicant is merely claiming that concept: (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. In such situations, the claim is considered to recite a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process on a generic computer
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed steps are human cognitive actions merely performed on general-purpose computer hardware, the claim can be directed to an abstract idea (mental process) even though performed on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Voter Verified (voting/verifying/submitting are human cognitive actions) and Versata (determining a price using general-purpose computer hardware); courts characterized these as directed to abstract ideas despite computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process in a computer environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite processes in a computer environment but that are analogous to human mental decisionmaking can be directed to mental-process-type abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Symantec (electronic post office analogous to deciding to read/dispose of mail) and FairWarning (fraud-detection rules that mirror human questions asked for detecting misuse). Examiners should determine whether, aside from generic computer steps, the claims could be performed mentally or with pen and paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely use a computer as a tool to perform a concept that humans could perform without a computer are directed to mental processes/abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping performed by humans) and Berkheimer (parsing and comparing data recited at a high level of generality). If the computer only facilitates the human-conducted concept, the claim may be an abstract mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both product and process claims may recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Product claims (e.g., computer systems, computer-readable media) as well as process claims can recite mental processes and thus be directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Content Extraction (API extracting info from documents), Mortgage Grader (computer system and method), CyberSource (computer-readable medium for fraud detection), Symantec (post office system), Voter Verified (self-verifying voting system), Electric Power Group (monitoring system), Versata (computer-readable storage media). Examiners should understand 'mental processes' as a type of abstract idea, not as a statutory claim category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative abstract ideas (non-enumerated exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In rare circumstances, a claim limitation may be treated as an abstract idea even though it does not fall within the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes); such a limitation is a 'tentative abstract idea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the claim under the eligibility framework: if the claim integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → Step 2A:NO → eligible at Pathway B. If not integrated → Step 2A:YES → proceed to Step 2B: if claim provides an inventive concept → eligible at Pathway C; if not → bring application to Technology Center (TC) director. A Step 2B rejection based on a tentative abstract idea requires TC director approval (to be reflected by form paragraph 7.05.017 and TC Director signature). Interviews with the examiner may help; TC Director interview not required to withdraw or maintain such a rejection but TC approval is required for issuance of the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have described these exceptions with terms like 'physical phenomena,' 'scientific principles,' 'natural laws,' and 'products of nature.' The basic tools of scientific/technological work (manifestations of laws of nature) are not patentable because they are part of the storehouse of knowledge. Examples and case citations are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of laws of nature/natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts have identified various concepts/products as laws of nature or natural phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples enumerated include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned farm animal (Roslin), correlations in DNA (Genetic Techs.), correlations from metabolism (Mayo/Prometheus), correlations between biomarker and disease risk (Cleveland Clinic), electromagnetism for signal transmission (O’Reilly v. Morse), bacterial qualities (Funk Bros.), primers (Ambry Genetics), chemical principles (Tilghman), cell-free fetal DNA (Ariosa), genotype–drug response correlation (Vanda), etc. These examples illustrate the kinds of subject matter courts have treated as natural-law or natural-phenomenon exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims describing natural abilities/processes are not always laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every claim that describes a natural ability or process necessarily recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon; claims focused on applications or particular process steps may be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect (fractionating/recovering/cryopreserving hepatocytes found eligible because not merely observing a property), methods of treating cancer with chemotherapy and methods of producing a new compound are not per se laws of nature when the claim is focused on applied treatment or manufacturing steps. Such claims proceed to Prong Two (Step 2A Prong Two) if another exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application can overcome a law of nature exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, the claim may still be eligible if it integrates the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Vanda — claims reciting a natural relationship between genotype and drug response were held eligible because they included a tailored treatment step that applied the relationship in a practical manner. This is equivalent to finding eligibility at Step 2A Prong Two (Pathway B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature as a category
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, courts often refer to the exception as a 'product of nature.' This includes isolated naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: isolated DNA (Myriad), primers (Ambry Genetics), bacterial mixtures (Funk Bros.), cloned animals (Roslin). Step 2A uses 'law of nature' and 'natural phenomenon' inclusively of 'products of nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-naturally occurring products lacking markedly different characteristics are excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Synthetic or artificially created products that are structurally identical or lack markedly different characteristics from naturally occurring counterparts are treated as products of nature and may be ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambry Genetics teaches that synthetically replicated gene sequences identical to natural sequences are not patent eligible. Creating a product by human ingenuity does not automatically make it eligible; the key is whether it possesses 'markedly different characteristics' from a natural counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis determines whether a nature-based product is a 'product of nature' exception by comparing the claimed product to its naturally occurring counterpart; it is part of Step 2A Prong One.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart, the claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Pathway B (Step 2A:NO), unless the claim recites another exception. If the entire claim is a single nature-based product and markedly different characteristics are shown, no further analysis (Step 2B) is necessary. If the nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics, the claim recites a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied only to the nature-based product limitations in a claim, and not extended to products that are not nature-based when viewed as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care should be taken not to overly extend the analysis: apply it only to nature-based product limitations (e.g., a claimed 'Lactobacillus bacterium' or 'probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk'). If the limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the analysis because it is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product (i.e., a product of nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI and nature-based product limitations may encompass eligible and ineligible embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), a nature-based product limitation may encompass both embodiments that are markedly different (eligible) and embodiments that lack markedly different characteristics (products of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When BRI encompasses both eligible and ineligible products, examiners should point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments, if possible, to claim embodiments that are not products of nature. Examiners should consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP § 2106.06) is appropriate for inventions that clearly do not seek to tie up judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis for clear non-tie-up cases
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites a nature-based product limitation but is directed to an invention that clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception, the examiner should consider the streamlined eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2106.06; in such cases it may not be necessary to conduct the markedly different characteristics analysis.
